quote: “Ils opèrent en particulier dans la partie … Λⁿ_A M”

sentences: For a free rank-\(n\) module, the image of \(\operatorname{Alt}=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\sigma\) is the free line generated by the alternating basis tensor, which has a coefficient \(1\), so \(\Lambda^nM\) embeds in \(M^{\otimes n}\) without inverting \(n!\).
Every tensor endomorphism commuting with the permutations preserves that image, and localization gives the finite-projective version; the full proof is NORM01 in the norm memorandum.
This differs from identifying the exterior power with the whole sign-eigenspace, which has dimension \(3\), rather than \(1\), for \(M=\mathbf F_2^2\).
Thus Hua’s warning about the full eigenspace is correct, but its claimed need to abandon the integral image construction is too strong; Deligne (1973, XVII §6.3.1) is the published comparator.

context: Hua98, §§I, “Le déterminant…” and “La norme…,” pp. 2–4 (scans 003–005).

context: Hua98, normalization/additivity, pp. 6 and 11 (scans 007 and 012).

sentences: For \(B=B_1\times B_2\), block-diagonal multiplication gives \(N_{B/A}(b_1,b_2)=N_{B_1/A}(b_1)N_{B_2/A}(b_2)\), and the section lies in the \((r_1,r_2)\) component of the symmetric power of the disjoint union.
The rank-one identity is immediate, while degree zero gives the empty symmetric product and the chosen nullary value, which is the identity in the additive or multiplicative unital cases.
This verifies, rather than merely repeats, the additivity diagram used by Hua; the separate problem with a single numerical degree on the empty target is N10 (Deligne, 1973, XVII §6.3.5).

context: Hua98, “La transitivité,” pp. 4–8 and axiom (ii ter), p. 11 (scans 005–009,012).

sentences: For finite locally free \(A\to B\to C\), the required identity is \(N_{C/A}=N_{B/A}\circ N_{C/B}\), with the corresponding flattening of symmetric powers.
The norm memorandum proves it integrally by a block-determinant identity, using a monic-polynomial localization and then descent back to the original ring.
Because the proof works after every scalar extension, it establishes equality of polynomial laws and of the sections, a stronger check than agreement on geometric fibres alone.
This supplies the proof behind the manuscript’s final assertion and Hua’s reconstruction; the exact published comparator is Deligne (1973, XVII Lemma 6.3.3 and §6.3.15(v)).

Consequently their rank is \(\#(E^n/H)\), and this particular invariant module commutes with every base change, without inverting \(|H|\).
This rechecks Hua’s explicitly added argument and supplies the missing detail behind the manuscript’s ease assertion.
It must not be extended to arbitrary group actions: the involution \(\epsilon\mapsto-\epsilon\) on \(\mathbf Z[\epsilon]/\epsilon^2\) gains extra invariants modulo \(2\).

The source’s own later wording “dit de degré r” and Hua’s reported Lean predicate hasDeg suggest a suitable repair: treat degree as indexed data or a fibrewise predicate, which is vacuously true for every \(r\) over the empty target.
This differs from refuting the canonical-section construction or the uninspected Lean development.

The notation \(M^G\) here denotes the coinduced function module explicitly identified by the preceding Hom expression, not invariants.

An injective G-module is a retract of a coinduced module, and insertion of a chosen point contracts the resulting ordinary function-valued Čech complex; an arbitrary coinduced module need not itself be injective.
This supplies the details behind the source’s sketch and makes Hua’s shorthand explicit; see COH02–COH03 and Hochschild and Serre (1953, I §3).

Only when \(F'\triangleleft F\) does this become \(H^p(F/F',H^q(F',A))\Rightarrow H^{p+q}(F,A)\); without normality the stabilizers in the nerve must remain visible.
This checks Hua’s comparison with Hochschild–Serre under its actual group-quotient hypothesis (Hochschild & Serre, 1953, II §4).
